Unlawful Arrests

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
.....what you need to know about unlawful arrests in South Africa

Unique Selling Point:
An issue that affect each and everyone in South Africa

Summary:
Unlawful arrest and detention are very common in South Africa. So much so that over the last few years SAPS had to pay out in excess of R1,5 billion rand in claims for this, with another R30 billion in claims pending.

It also now transpires that many of these wrongful arrests have been encouraged by illegal instructions from a wide variety of role players within the Police – from divisional commanders to unit commanders. They among other things, set quotas and issued instructions to police on the ground to make arrests which are clearly unlawful. (there are very strict laws governing arrest as it is seen as a measure of last resort). A recent circular by the National Commissioner has now prohibited these instructions (there is a whole list he mentions), and the primary motivation is the recent Constitutional Court ruling that SAPS is responsible for the whole time a person remains in unlawful arrest. This could double or triple the liability of the Minister of Police. The quantum of the claims dwindles into insignificance if the legal costs are added to the picture.


Further information:
Unlawful arrest and detention are very common in South Africa. So much so that over the last few years SAPS had to pay out in excess of R1,5 billion rand in claims for this, with another R30 billion in claims pending.

It also now transpires that many of these wrongful arrests have been encouraged by illegal instructions from a wide variety of role players within the Police – from divisional commanders to unit commanders. They among other things, set quotas and issued instructions to police on the ground to make arrests which are clearly unlawful. (there are very strict laws governing arrest as it is seen as a measure of last resort). A recent circular by the National Commissioner has now prohibited these instructions (there is a whole list he mentions), and the primary motivation is the recent Constitutional Court ruling that SAPS is responsible for the whole time a person remains in unlawful arrest. This could double or triple the liability of the Minister of Police. The quantum of the claims dwindles into insignificance if the legal costs are added to the picture.

Furthermore, being arrested and detained is a traumatic experience to say the least and is used by the Police to intimidate and to punish people, instead of using for what it is intended for. There are very strict rules around arrest in the Criminal Procedures Act, that police cannot suspend on a whim.

We have a number case studies who are textbook cases of these excesses meted out by SAPS:
• Kobus Oosthuizen who was unlawfully arrested and badly beaten up and deliberately hit with a car (we have video and photographs)
• Mr Appelgryn was arrested after he fired a gun in self-defence
• Mr Roos was arrested when a pedestrian ran into the side of his car on the highway. He was not in any way at fault, yet he was arrested.
• Mr Gerald Visser who was arrested without a warrant or cause and detained in cells and denied medication for a serious heart condition.
• We also have several arrests on video that did the rounds on social media

We have two legal specialists on board:
• Attorney Jear-Ray Pearton of Gildenhuys Malatji Incorporated, who deals with this on a regular basis. Sharp a tack and knows what goes down. He has many clients whom he helped to get compensation. Not positive about what can be done – he says make sure you have a lawyer on speed dial.
• Advocate Johan Gaum. He is an ex-policeman and specializes in unlawful arrest cases. He is THE go-to guy in this field and feels strongly about the issue. Very passionate.

And we will have to get comments on the issue from SAPS as well.

Other layers:
• Basic principle: Investigate to arrest, not arrest to investigate
• Arrests and detention by Traffic and Metro Police – where does that fit in?
• There is actually loose rue of thumb governing compensation for arrests (R40 000 per night)
• What to do when threatened with arrest?

Press Release:


Unlawful Arrests
Tens of thousands of South Africans have been unlawfully been arrested and detained by the SAPS over the last few years. Courts have ordered the police service to pay out 1,5 billion rands in compensation the last few years – with at least a further R30 billion in claims and legal costs pending. Carte Blanche examines the implications of a recent Constitutional Court ruling that the police are responsible for the whole period of a suspect’s unlawful arrest and ask what it will take to reverse the trend?
Producer: Eugene Botha| Presenter: Derek Watts


Script:


V/O:
This CCTV footage shows an altercation in a parking lot.

The moment the man is down, attackers jump him, and viciously beat him.
LINK:
This video is, to say the least, disturbing. But what is even more disturbing is the conduct of the police who arrived on the scene.
V/O:
They can be seen walking into picture, seemingly not at all concerned about the unconscious man at their feet.
Kobus:
I thought I was going to die.
V/O:
Kobus Oosthuizen is the victim in the video. He says he was first attacked for no reason in a nearby restaurant.
Kobus:
I was seriously assaulted by 3 men.
LINK:
Oosthuizen managed to break loose and fled to the outside of the restaurant, followed by his attackers. He says there he fired two warning shots into the ground, and they retreated.
Kobus:
I asked them “Why? Why did you assault me so unnecessarily up there?”
V/O:
That was when the car hit him, and the assault resumed. When he came to, he discovered the police had handcuffed him.
Kobus:
They did not ask any questions, they immediately handcuffed me. I was covered in blood.
V/O:
Seriously injured, Oosthuizen says he was taken to hospital in an ambulance, but before he could be admitted, the police transferred him to a car, and drove to Sinoville Police Station. There they did not take a statement, and did not read him his rights. Locked in a cell, and in great pain, he begged for medical attention throughout the night but only received treatment the following day.

He was charged with unlawfully discharging a firearm but as it was in self-defence, he was acquitted. He has now instituted a civil claim against the Minister of Police for unlawful arrest and detention.

But, Oosthuizen’s case is not an isolated incident.
LINK:
Civil claims against the police for misconduct have been mounting and involves staggering amounts of money.
Over last few years the South African Police Service has paid out one point five billion rand to victims of police misconduct. The bulk of this was the result of unlawful arrests and detentions.

The police stopped reporting on the exact nature of civil claims, but in 2016, 86% of these claims were for unlawful arrest and detention.

And all pending claims against the Police could be as high as 30 billion rand, if all legal fees are included. The problem is further exacerbated by the inability of some state attorneys to defend even spurious claims effectively.

Attorney Jean-Ray Pearton of Pretoria says the actual number of unlawful arrest cases is staggering.
Jean-Ray:
These are not strictly speaking large quantum amounts. You are looking at a rule of thumb, if you are lucky, for a night in detention, between five and forty thousand rand. So the numbers you need to running through the court system, to rack up the debt they have in making payments are huge.
V/O:
Advocate Johann Gaum has been instituting civil claims against the Police for unlawful arrest and detention for decades.
Derek:
So, obviously, big mistakes are being made on a regular basis.

Johan:
Serious mistakes. It is fair to say it, and it is escalating.

V/O:
Gaum says that because arrest infringes so fundamentally on a person’s human rights, it is carefully defined in the Criminal Procedure Act. All law enforcement officials, including Metro and Traffic Police must adhere to the stipulations.

According to the Act, the Police can arrest you with a valid warrant of arrest, or without a warrant, if a crime was committed in their presence.

Further, if a Police official has reasonable grounds to believe that you committed a Schedule 1 offence, which is a serious offence, they may also arrest you without a warrant. But, they cannot arrest you on a whim. The Act views arrest in a very serious light.
Johan:
It constitutes one of the most drastic infringements on the rights of an individual and a member should therefore regard it as the last resort

Derek:
In many cases it’s the first resort?

Johan:
Well I find in many cases it is the first resort.
V/O:
Immanuel Tseisa, a lawyer from Pretoria, fell victim to an unlawful arrest after a soccer match.
Immanuel:
We came back to the office and then we were having social, it was inside the premises of the law firm.
V/O:
He was standing outside their building with colleagues, when a convoy of police vehicles arrived and a police officer approached them.
Immanuel:
He said to us we received a complaint that from 3 ‘o’ clock or 4 o’clock, people have been making noise. Then all of a sudden he said all of you get in line. So I was turning, I wanted to obey his command. When I was turning then he just said to those guys: “Even this one take him.” He said I was being disrespectful. Without me saying a word, without me saying anything, I was just standing.
V/O:
At the Police station the arresting officers did not take statements and no case was opened against him. Tseisa spent most of the night detained. He subsequently sued the Minster of Police and received a substantial amount in compensation.

That the high numbers of unlawful arrests are a concern for the South African Police is evident in a letter addressed to all members in November last year.
LINK:
This is the circular that was sent out by the National Commissioner. It makes for interesting, but also disturbing reading.
It admonishes Police members to stick to the letter of the law when effecting arrests. It also refers to a recent Constitutional Court ruling that now holds the Police liable for compensation for the whole period a person is detained because of an unlawful arrest. In the past they were only liable for compensation for a maximum of 48 hours. This new ruling could increase the quantum of claims against the police substantially.

It further indicates that some Police Commanders have been issuing unlawful instructions to members relating to arrest. Among others, he mentions instructions to fulfil arrest quotas, and directives to arrest people in the middle of the night simply to humiliate them.
Derek:
Johan, should we be concerned about the contents of the letter from the National Commissioner?

Johan:
I am seriously concerned because, it means that unlawful orders were issued by senior police officials, like provincial commissioners, to affect unlawful arrests, to infringe on citizens or members of the public’s human right to freedom.
Jean-Ray:
Your right to liberty is one of the most jealously guarded rights in the Constitution.
V/O:
Brigadier Vish Naidoo, the National Police Spokesperson stated that they were not prepared to grant media interviews relating to the letter.

He also added:
“You may notice that, on the circular which you are referring to, nowhere is it addressed to the media. This document was intended only for consumption of members of the SAPS to mitigate potential risks which police management has identified.”
LINK:
Apart from the South African Police the Metro and Traffic are also involved in affecting arrests.
V/O:
Shirley Sporen was stopped by Police in Irene in early January. She did not have her he driver’s license with her. When pulled over, she put her phone on “record”.
Officer:
Are you taking a video?

Shirley:
I have to darling.

Officer:
But I have to write you a ticket.

Shirley:
It’s fine.

Officer:
But you don’t have a right.

Derek:
Can you film the police during an arrest?

Johan:
As long as it is in a public place.
Shirley:
Then a male officer came and he said something to her in another language and as soon as he had said something to her, her whole attitude changed towards me.

Officer:
You’re driving without a licence then you are taking police pictures, then you tell us you are scared? For what?

V/O:
And then they arrested her.
Shirley:
I said to her, “Please can I just phone my husband, please! Mommy’s gone to the shop, to go get her medicine and I need to tell my children and husband mommy’s not coming home. Because I’m being taken away.” She said no.
V/O:
Sporen says she carted to two Police stations and was eventually released on bail, charged with Crimen Injuria for insulting police officers. That was 4 weeks ago, and the Police have yet to take a statement. She is due back in court in mid-February.
LINK:
The big question of course is, what can, or should one do when a law enforcement official wants to arrest you?
Johan:
Yes, you may resist an unlawful arrest, but then you run the risk of injury, obviously….

Jean-Ray:
Let’s face it once you’ve been arrested, you are in trouble. You odds are stacked against you, if you are arrested and you are in detention, someone needs to intervene.

Derek:
Sounds like a frightening scenario to me.

Jean-Ray:
Yes.

It also now transpires that many of these wrongful arrests have been encouraged by illegal instructions from a wide variety of role players within the Police – from divisional commanders to unit commanders. They among other things, set quotas and issued instructions to police on the ground to make arrests which are clearly unlawful. (there are very strict laws governing arrest as it is seen as a measure of last resort). A recent circular by the National Commissioner has now prohibited these instructions (there is a whole list he mentions), and the primary motivation is the recent Constitutional Court ruling that SAPS is responsible for the whole time a person remains in unlawful arrest. This could double or triple the liability of the Minister of Police. The quantum of the claims dwindles into insignificance if the legal costs are added to the picture. Furthermore, being arrested and detained is a traumatic experience to say the least and is used by the Police to intimidate and to punish people, instead of using for what it is intended for. There are very strict rules around arrest in the Criminal Procedures Act, that police cannot suspend on a whim. We have a number case studies who are textbook cases of these excesses meted out by SAPS: • Kobus Oosthuizen who was unlawfully arrested and badly beaten up and deliberately hit with a car (we have video and photographs) • Mr Appelgryn was arrested after he fired a gun in self-defence • Mr Roos was arrested when a pedestrian ran into the side of his car on the highway. He was not in any way at fault, yet he was arrested. • Mr Gerald Visser who was arrested without a warrant or cause and detained in cells and denied medication for a serious heart condition. • We also have several arrests on video that did the rounds on social media We have two legal specialists on board: • Attorney Jear-Ray Pearton of Gildenhuys Malatji Incorporated, who deals with this on a regular basis. Sharp a tack and knows what goes down. He has many clients whom he helped to get compensation. Not positive about what can be done – he says make sure you have a lawyer on speed dial. • Advocate Johan Gaum. He is an ex-policeman and specializes in unlawful arrest cases. He is THE go-to guy in this field and feels strongly about the issue. Very passionate. And we will have to get comments on the issue from SAPS as well. Other layers: • Basic principle: Investigate to arrest, not arrest to investigate • Arrests and detention by Traffic and Metro Police – where does that fit in? • There is actually loose rue of thumb governing compensation for arrests (R40 000 per night) • What to do when threatened with arrest?
